What time is it?

A lesson about asking for the time, understanding the answer, and saying the hour clearly—including which part of the day it is.

After this lesson: the learner can ask “What time is it?”, understand a whole-hour answer, and reply “It is seven o’clock” or “It is three o’clock in the afternoon.”

A clock showing 7:00 represents seven o’clock. It cannot teach the meaning of o’clock as an isolated object label. Teach the expression inside an actual answer.

Lesson boundary

Time is the whole task.

  • Ask the time and take turns answering.
  • Read whole hours on clear analog and digital clocks.
  • Distinguish morning, afternoon, evening and night.
  • Connect a.m. / p.m. notation to the spoken answer.
  • Practise different hours using the numbers already learned.

Content changes

Give those minutes back to time practice.

  • Replace the standalone “O’clock” teaching card with a complete question → answer pair.
  • Replace “I wake up at seven o’clock” and “I study at night” in every affected section with time exchanges.
  • Keep daily routines in their own lessons. “At + activity time” is outside this lesson’s purpose.
  • Keep minutes, half past and quarter past for the later precision-time course.

The essential contrast

The same clock face. Two different times of day.

Both clocks point to three. An analog dial alone cannot tell us whether it is a.m. or p.m.; the learner needs explicit time-of-day evidence.

3:00 a.m.

It is three o’clock
in the morning.

Son las tres de la madrugada.

Early morning can still be dark. Darkness alone does not mean p.m.

3:00 p.m.

It is three o’clock
in the afternoon.

Son las tres de la tarde.

Teach the hour first; then keep that hour and change only its day context.

Notation support: a.m. runs from midnight until before noon; p.m. runs from noon until before midnight. First practise 3 a.m. versus 3 p.m. and 7 a.m. versus 7 p.m. Explain the 12 a.m. / 12 p.m. boundary in help before testing it. “Noon” and “midnight” are support explanations here, not new assessed vocabulary.

The learning sequence

Introduce → distinguish → understand → say → build.

Use one connected exchange at a time. The question and its answer occupy separate adjacent slides, with the same asking/responding roles and a clock close-up for the answer. Each section follows the same conceptual arc while changing what the learner does.

1. Learn

Seven question → answer pairs: basic hour, morning, afternoon, evening, night, a.m. and p.m. Every answer is a complete sentence.

Approved allocation: 14 slides

2. Recognize

Match clocks to full answers. Begin with two choices. Change the hour first; hold it constant to contrast day periods next.

Approved allocation: 10 slides

3. Listen

Hear time answers without their transcripts. Choose the corresponding clock or digital time. Include spoken two-person exchanges.

Approved allocation: 10 slides

4. Speak

Eight cards practise the question and full time answers. Learners produce both asking and answering language.

Approved allocation: 8 slides

5. Use

Complete four two-word gaps, then build four full questions or answers, including a.m. and p.m.

Approved allocation: 8 slides

Approved and implemented allocation: 50 purposeful cards. The shared practice audit verifies each new target across the required stages. Counts follow meaningful practice and the existing shared formats. Distribute hours 1–12 through practice rather than adding twelve identical Learn introductions.

Language contract

Teach useful chunks.

What time is it?
It is seven o’clock.
It is three o’clock in the afternoon.
It is seven o’clock in the evening.
It is nine o’clock at night.

Reuse learned numbers, it / is, in / the and morning. Declare the new question, o’clock, afternoon, evening, night, at inside at night, and notation a.m. / p.m.—eight targets under the current lesson budget. Treat evening and the notation as additions requiring explicit first teaching.

For this introductory lesson, use one answer form consistently. Everyday “It’s…” and “It is three p.m.” can be introduced as alternatives after the core form is secure; do not use untaught alternatives as distractors.

Visual & voice contract

The evidence must match the words.

  • Large, numbered clock dials. Minute hand at 12; hour hand exactly at the stated hour.
  • Asker looks at the listener and naturally asks; responder checks or indicates the same clock. Keep faces, clothing and setting continuous across the two shots.
  • Show a.m. / p.m. or another explicit reviewed time cue when day period matters. A sun or moon by itself is insufficient for the 3 a.m. case.
  • Keep question and answer voices attached to their actual speakers when roles switch.
  • During listening assessment, hide the answer phrase. Replay repeats the exact English cue.
  • Keep complete clocks and day cues visible at phone framing; do not reuse the already documented cropped-clock option.

Acceptance criteria

What would make the revised lesson ready?

  • No standalone “O’clock” teaching or assessment target; each occurrence belongs to a complete time answer.
  • No routine, activity-at-time, weekday or schedule tasks in 4.10.
  • Each new target is taught before it appears in a correct answer, distractor, audio line or construction.
  • At least five meaningful practice encounters across four sections for each new target, adjusted to the existing practice audit’s rules. Count correct-path evidence, not metadata.
  • The successful path practises both asking and answering, different whole hours, and same-hour a.m. / p.m. contrasts.
  • Every clock and time-of-day cue agrees with its exact sentence; answer choices have one defensible correct answer.
  • Both clients retain the shared lesson engine, help, replay, pronunciation and Completa behavior. Verify phone portrait and landscape, wrong answers, retry and completion.
